security_spec.violation_condition: In the Linux kernel (via SBI/SEE firmware), after mnstatus.NMIE is set to 1, the one-way enable latch prevents software from masking RNMIs; if the M-mode RNMI handler fails to properly save/restore all interrupted context through mnscratch, or if the mnepc WARL silently remaps a valid kernel resume PC into a different invalid address on a bogus handler write, the kernel resumes at an unintended instruction with corrupted register state.
security_spec.summary: Smrnmi CSRs and mnret are M-mode-only; kernel relies on firmware to correctly save/restore context in mnscratch and not corrupt mnepc across WARL remapping — any firmware bug silently corrupts kernel execution on mnret resume

findings.finding: The Smrnmi extension CSRs (mnepc, mncause, mnstatus, mnscratch) and the MNRET instruction are M-mode-only constructs. They are managed entirely by the M-mode firmware/SEE (e.g., OpenSBI). The Linux kernel runs in S-mode and has no code referencing any RNMI CSR, register, or handler logic. A comprehensive grep across arch/riscv/, include/, drivers/firmware/, and Documentation/ confirms zero matches for mnepc, mncause, mnstatus, mnscratch, MNRET, RNMI, NMIE, smrnmi, or resumable NMI. This is architecturally correct — S-mode software cannot access these M-mode CSRs and RNMI handling is the firmware's responsibility.
findings.snippet: (no relevant kernel code exists — Smrnmi is an M-mode/firmware concern)

spec_citations.excerpt: The Smrnmi extension adds support for resumable non-maskable interrupts (RNMIs) to RISC-V. The extension adds four new CSRs (mnepc, mncause, mnstatus, and mnscratch) to hold the interrupted state, and one new instruction, MNRET, to resume from the RNMI handler.
The hart then enters machine-mode and jumps to the RNMI trap handler address.
